_readme.covers: Modal progressions in minor keys (the natural-minor VII/VI complex, Dorian v and iv), modal-mixture extensions in major (bVII, bIII, bVI as idiomatic colours), chromatic-modal transitions (diminished sevenths as passing and neighbour chords), common-tone diminished sevenths, and applied chords targeting modal degrees. This pass exists because passes 1-6 enumerated common-practice diatonic and chromatic progressions but never covered the modal layer of the vocabulary, which appears constantly in chorales, folk-influenced writing, and nineteenth-century repertoire.
_readme.structure: Each rule has: id, quality, from, to, feedback.

matching.from: Root numerals for the previous chord.
matching.to: Root numerals for the current chord.
matching.bare_root: A bare numeral like 'VII' matches any inversion.
matching.figured: A numeral with a figure like 'VII7' matches only that inversion.
matching.applied: Applied chords are written with a slash, e.g. 'V/bVII'.
matching.modal_notation: In minor keys, VII (uppercase) is the natural subtonic on the lowered seventh degree; III is the natural mediant; VI is the natural submediant. v (lowercase) is the Dorian/natural-minor dominant.

how_to_add_a_rule: 1. Copy a rule block between { and }.
2. Give it a new unique id.
3. Set from and to as above.
4. Pick a quality: excellent, good, fair, discouraged, bad.
6. Save. No trailing comma after the last rule.

rules.feedback: Subtonic to tonic — a modal cadence. The lowered seventh approaches the tonic by whole step rather than by the leading-tone half step. Idiomatic in modal, folk, and Renaissance-derived writing; in tonal common-practice it produces a close that is settled but not fully functional.

Subtonic seventh resolving to tonic. The chord looks like a dominant seventh but lacks the leading tone, so the resolution is modal rather than functional. Common in Baroque sequences and a hallmark of the descending-fifths chain.

Subtonic to submediant — the first step of the natural-minor descending tetrachord in the bass. A modal descent that avoids the raised leading tone, characteristic of Aeolian and Dorian cadential approaches.
Submediant to subtonic. Approaches a modal cadence by ascending step. The VII that follows can resolve to i (modal cadence) or continue descending to VI again (a back-and-forth neighbour motion).
Subtonic to mediant. A modal ascent to the relative major, idiomatic in natural minor and Dorian. The motion is stepwise in the bass and prepares a cadence in III.

Mediant to subtonic — bIII to bVII in the home mode. A modal step-down, idiomatic in modal and folk-influenced writing; less common in functional common-practice harmony where the mediant typically returns to VI or proceeds to IV.
Minor (modal) dominant to tonic — a Dorian or Aeolian cadence. Without the raised leading tone, the resolution is softer than a harmonic-minor V–i; the modal colour is deliberate.
Tonic to minor (modal) dominant. The ear hears the dominant degree without the leading-tone pull of a major V; a Dorian-flavoured motion, common in modal and folk-influenced writing.
Minor dominant to minor subdominant — a Dorian motion. The chord moves against the expected functional flow but is idiomatic in modal contexts where the dominant degree lacks its tonic-dominant pull.
Minor subdominant to minor (modal) dominant. Dorian-flavoured stepwise motion into the modal dominant; frequent in nineteenth-century modal-inflected passages.
Minor subdominant to subtonic. The motion prepares a modal cadence on i (or I) using the lowered seventh degree. Very common in Bach and in folk-influenced writing.
Subtonic to minor subdominant. Backward motion within the modal vocabulary; idiomatic in the middle of a phrase but rarely at cadences.
Flat-VII to tonic in a major key. A mixture borrowing from the parallel minor; the modal close is warm and settled rather than driven. Common in nineteenth-century and popular idioms.
Flat-III to subdominant. Mixture colour from the parallel minor; the bass ascends by whole step from the borrowed mediant into the subdominant area, a hallmark of extended mixture in major keys.
Flat-VI to dominant. The lowered sixth degree descends by step to 5 while the bass ascends, producing a strong chromatic approach to the cadence. A standard mixture cadential preparation.
Flat-VI to flat-VII. A chromatic-modal step-up preparing the return to I, characteristically used in the extended plagal close of the nineteenth-century repertoire.
Flat-VII to flat-VI. The reverse of the bVI–bVII pair; less common but idiomatic in chromatic descents to the subdominant.
Submediant to applied leading-tone seventh of the subtonic. The diminished seventh acts as a chromatic passing chord between VI and VII, intensifying the modal cadence.

Applied leading-tone seventh resolving to the subtonic. The applied leading tone rises by half step to the root of VII while the chordal seventh falls, producing a striking chromatic intensification of the modal cadence.
Minor subdominant to applied leading-tone seventh of V. A chromatic pre-cadential move that combines mixture with an applied diminished seventh; common in nineteenth-century cadential preparation.
Applied leading-tone seventh resolving to V. All four voices move by half step or common tone into the dominant; a standard chromatic preparation for the cadence.
Tonic to the diatonic leading-tone seventh. Approaching a diminished seventh by step or common tone; the chord acts as a chromatic intensification of the dominant that follows.

Diatonic leading-tone seventh resolving to tonic in minor. The leading tone rises, the chordal seventh (the lowered sixth degree) falls, and the chord resolves into the tonic triad. A defining gesture of the minor mode.

Common-tone diminished seventh built on the raised fourth degree, approached from the tonic. The chord shares a common tone with the tonic triad and functions as a chromatic decoration before returning to I or I6.

Common-tone diminished seventh returning to the tonic. The chord is a chromatic neighbour that shares one common tone with the preceding tonic triad; its other voices move chromatically and resolve back into the tonic.
Applied dominant of the flat subtonic. In a major key this tonicizes the borrowed subtonic; the resolution is idiomatic in mixture-flavoured passages and in popular-influenced writing.
Applied dominant of the flat mediant. Tonicizes the borrowed mediant; common in nineteenth-century chromatic passages preparing the shift to the parallel minor's relative major.
Applied dominant of the flat submediant. Tonicizes the borrowed submediant; a standard chromatic preparation for the mixture-flavoured cadential approach bVI–V–i (or bVI–V–I).

Flat-VII to I — a modal close borrowed from the Mixolydian mode. Frequent in folk-influenced writing and in the blues idiom; produces a warm, settled cadence without the leading-tone drive of a functional V–I.
Subtonic to submediant — the second step of the natural-minor descending tetrachord. If the bass then continues to V and to iv, the entire descent outlines the modal plagal close i–VII–VI–V.
